paragraphs: A density estimator describes how likely different combinations of variables are. NADE and its real-valued counterpart RNADE do this using a fixed ordering of the variables. That ordering affects which questions are easy to answer: conditioning on early variables and marginalizing later ones is straightforward, while other arrangements require approximate inference.

The paper introduces a training procedure that shares parameters across NADE models for every possible variable ordering. This makes it possible to train those models together efficiently. For a particular inference task, the method can then use an ordering that makes the requested calculation convenient. Different orderings also provide models that can be combined into an ensemble.

The procedure additionally supports deep models, extending beyond the training approach of the original NADE. Experiments report state-of-the-art density estimation performance from ensembles of Deep NADE models. The contribution therefore connects flexible inference with stronger density modeling: parameter sharing makes many useful orderings available, while the training method accommodates deeper networks.
icml-2014-a-deep-and-tractable-density-e.tldr: Shared training across variable orderings makes deep NADE models flexible for inference and enables high-performing density estimation ensembles.

paragraphs: Grouped data can carry information at two levels: the observations inside each group and the context describing the group itself. This paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric model that uses both. It simultaneously discovers compact structure in group contents and clusters the groups, allowing contextual information to contribute to the organization of the data.

The construction uses Dirichlet processes with a nested product base measure to represent observations at multiple levels. Its relationship to established models helps explain what the combination accomplishes. Integrating out the contents leaves a Dirichlet process mixture over contexts; integrating out group-specific contexts leaves a nested Dirichlet process mixture over contents. Both views are therefore contained within one framework.

The authors provide a Polya-urn interpretation and an efficient collapsed Gibbs procedure for inference. Experiments on real-world text and image datasets demonstrate advantages from incorporating context through this model. The findings support treating group descriptions and internal observations as complementary evidence when learning both group clusters and the structure within them.
icml-2014-bayesian-nonparametric-multile.tldr: A multilevel Bayesian clustering model combines group contents with contextual information and connects two established Dirichlet process constructions.

paragraphs: Natural actor-critic algorithms update a policy using an estimated natural policy gradient. This paper examines whether several popular methods actually estimate the intended gradient without bias in the discounted reward setting. It shows that NAC-LSTD and eNAC, among others, fail to provide unbiased estimates despite claims that they do.

The authors derive unbiased natural actor-critic methods for discounted rewards using both batch and iterative gradient estimation. This addresses the mismatch between the quantity existing algorithms claim to estimate and the estimates they produce. They also argue that the identified bias makes those existing algorithms more appropriate for average reward problems, distinguishing two reward objectives that require different treatment.

A separate theoretical result concerns global optimality. Under conditions where Sarsa(lambda) is guaranteed to reach an optimal policy, the authors show that the natural actor-critic objective is concave. Policy gradient methods consequently also receive a global convergence guarantee in that setting. This conclusion depends on the stated condition; it does not establish global convergence for policy gradient methods in general.
icml-2014-bias-in-natural-actor-critic-a.tldr: The paper identifies bias in popular discounted reward natural actor-critics, derives unbiased alternatives, and establishes a conditional global convergence result.

paragraphs: In online multiclass prediction, a learner repeatedly chooses among several labels. Under bandit feedback, it learns only whether its chosen label was correct. A wrong prediction does not reveal the true label, making the available feedback less informative than in ordinary online classification and making effective learning algorithms harder to design.

This paper proposes a systematic way to construct multiclass bandit learners from existing online binary classifiers. The approach follows boosting: several component learners are combined to produce a stronger learner. Its theoretical foundation is a specified weak-learning condition on those binary classifiers. When that condition holds, combining them allows the construction of a bandit learner with arbitrarily strong performance in the sense established by the theory.

Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution matters because it gives a reusable route from binary learning methods to a more restricted feedback setting. The guarantee remains conditional on the weak-learning requirement, so the result does not imply that any arbitrary collection of binary classifiers will suffice.
icml-2014-boosting-with-online-binary-le.tldr: Boosting converts online binary classifiers satisfying a weak-learning condition into strong multiclass predictors that need only correctness feedback.

paragraphs: A full ranking contains many comparisons between alternatives. Rank breaking converts it into counts of pairwise comparisons associated with particular ranking positions. These simpler observations can support estimation through the Generalized Method of Moments, which can offer substantial computational savings over maximum likelihood while retaining comparable statistical efficiency.

The paper studies which ways of breaking rankings preserve consistency for random utility models, including Plackett-Luce and Normal-RUM. Consistency matters because a convenient computational shortcut should still approach the intended model parameters as data accumulate. The authors characterize valid breakings and give a general sufficient condition under which full breaking is the only consistent choice. That condition is sufficient, rather than a claim that full breaking is always necessary.

The analysis also provides a three-way classification theorem for single-edge breakings. Experiments assess the proposed method's computational efficiency and statistical performance. Together, these results make rank breaking a more principled estimation tool: the choice of pairwise information is governed by statistical validity as well as by computational convenience.
icml-2014-computing-parametric-ranking-m.tldr: The paper characterizes when splitting rankings into pairwise counts yields consistent, computationally efficient estimates of parametric ranking models.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification assigns a set of labels to an example, and different applications judge those sets using different criteria. This paper formalizes a learning setup that incorporates the chosen evaluation criterion as a cost. Its aim is to support varied criteria systematically, instead of requiring a separate specialized algorithm for each one.

The proposed condensed filter tree converts the problem into cost-sensitive multiclass classification. It does so through the label powerset, where possible combinations of labels become classes. This creates an immediate computational challenge because the number of combinations grows exponentially. The method addresses representation, training, and prediction through a carefully designed tree that concentrates on key nodes.

Experiments across many real-world datasets find that the method is competitive with specialized algorithms on their particular criteria and performs better on general criteria. These results support the practical value of a common framework for differing application objectives. The stated contribution is an algorithm for optimizing arbitrary criteria within the cost-sensitive setup, supported by those empirical comparisons.
icml-2014-condensed-filter-tree-for-cost.tldr: Condensed filter trees make cost-sensitive multi-label learning practical across varied evaluation criteria by organizing the exponentially large label powerset.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with continuous actions requires a way to improve decisions across a continuous range of possibilities. This paper studies policy gradients for deterministic policies, which select a particular action for a given state. The key result is a simple gradient form expressed through the expected gradient of the action-value function.

That form allows the deterministic policy gradient to be estimated much more efficiently than the usual stochastic policy gradient. Exploration still needs explicit attention, because the policy being learned is deterministic. The authors introduce an off-policy actor-critic algorithm that learns this target policy from an exploratory behavior policy. The behavior policy supplies experience while the target policy is improved.

On several benchmark problems, deterministic policy gradient algorithms outperform their stochastic counterparts, with particularly strong results in high-dimensional action spaces. These findings support the practical significance of the efficient gradient form for continuous control. The paper's approach combines a deterministic decision rule with exploratory data collection, linking the mathematical result to an implementable learning algorithm.
icml-2014-deterministic-policy-gradient-.tldr: An efficiently estimable deterministic policy gradient supports off-policy actor-critic learning and performs especially well on benchmarks with high-dimensional actions.

paragraphs: Diagnosis and active learning can require a sequence of costly tests before an answer becomes certain. The paper models this as evaluating a discrete function by querying variables until the observed values uniquely determine its output. A decision tree specifies which variable to query next based on the answers already received.

There are two distinct cost objectives: keeping average expenditure low under a prior distribution and protecting against an expensive worst case. The proposed algorithm constructs one tree whose expected cost and worst-case cost are each within an O(log n) factor of their respective minimum possible values. The comparisons are to the best strategy for each objective, even though the algorithm must satisfy both guarantees simultaneously.

The paper also establishes that this approximation order cannot be improved to o(log n), assuming P differs from NP. The contribution therefore combines a constructive strategy with a matching computational barrier at the stated approximation scale. It provides simultaneous control of routine testing cost and worst-case expense within that guarantee.
icml-2014-diagnosis-determination-decisi.tldr: A decision-tree algorithm simultaneously approximates optimal expected and worst-case testing costs within the best possible logarithmic factor under P ≠ NP.

paragraphs: Spectral learning methods infer probabilistic models of variable-length strings using a Hankel matrix that records observed string frequencies. A singular value decomposition of this matrix supports learning a weighted automaton. Accuracy depends both on the information the matrix contains and on how closely its observed values track their expected values.

Earlier concentration bounds appear to worsen as the matrix becomes larger. This suggests a tension: retaining more string information could come with a weaker statistical guarantee. The paper develops dimension-free concentration bounds for several Hankel matrix variants, removing matrix size from this particular source of deterioration in the bounds.

Experiments show that the new bounds are tight and substantially improve on existing ones. The authors conclude that concentration around the mean does not itself provide an argument for restricting Hankel matrix size. This is a focused conclusion about statistical concentration, rather than a claim that every larger matrix necessarily produces a better learned model. It changes how the information-versus-size tradeoff should be interpreted.
icml-2014-dimension-free-concentration-b.tldr: Dimension-free bounds challenge the idea that larger Hankel matrices inherently suffer weaker statistical concentration in spectral learning.

paragraphs: Cross-validation helps select a kernel model by evaluating how it performs when portions of the data are withheld. Its computational burden comes from repeatedly training the learning algorithm. This paper proposes approximating the cross-validation criterion using a single solution of the underlying algorithm, reducing the need for repeated fitting.

The approach uses the Bouligand influence function, which describes how a solution responds to an infinitesimal contamination of the original distribution. The authors establish a connection between that local sensitivity and cross-validation. They relate the influence function to a first-order Taylor expansion, then calculate both the basic influence function and higher-order versions to build practical approximations of cross-validation error.

Experiments support the resulting criterion as sound and efficient. The central contribution is to turn information about how a fitted model changes under distributional perturbations into a cheaper model-selection calculation. The result remains an approximation to cross-validation, with the empirical findings supporting its usefulness rather than asserting exact equality with repeated training.
icml-2014-efficient-approximation-of-cro.tldr: Bouligand influence functions approximate cross-validation error for kernel methods using only one fitted solution of the learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Divergence estimation measures differences between probability distributions using observed data. A consistent estimator approaches the desired quantity as the sample grows, but consistency alone does not describe uncertainty at a finite sample size. This paper addresses that more specific question for an estimator of Renyi divergence.

Its main result is a finite-sample exponential concentration bound. Such a bound controls the probability that an estimate deviates from its target, providing a quantitative statement about estimation error before taking an infinite-data limit. The theorem applies to densities in a smooth Holder class defined on the d-dimensional unit cube. Smoothness and the specified domain are therefore part of the result's scope.

The authors identify the lack of such bounds for divergence estimators as a gap, qualified by their knowledge of prior work. They also provide a numerical experiment illustrating the theory. The contribution is principally a statistical guarantee for a particular estimator and density class, giving more precise control over finite-sample behavior than consistency by itself provides.
icml-2014-generalized-exponential-concen.tldr: The paper establishes a finite-sample exponential concentration bound for Renyi divergence estimation under specified smoothness and domain assumptions.

paragraphs: Clustering, segmentation, and change-point detection often partition data by minimizing Euclidean distortion. The resulting partitions depend on how differences between observations are measured. This paper learns a Mahalanobis metric for such problems, allowing the distance calculation to weight or select features in a way informed by relevant labeled examples.

Although the eventual partitioning problems are unsupervised, metric learning uses several fully or partially labeled datasets. A central assumption is that those datasets share the same metric. The authors formulate learning as large-margin structured prediction, with regularizers and losses chosen to produce a convex optimization problem that can be solved efficiently. This treats the desired partition as a structured output.

Experiments show significant improvements on bioinformatics tasks and on video or image segmentation. The findings indicate that learning the geometry used by a partitioning method can improve its results, especially when the problem has relevant structure. The contribution ties supervised information across datasets to the distance measure used in subsequent unsupervised partitioning.
icml-2014-large-margin-metric-learning-f.tldr: A convex large-margin formulation learns shared distance metrics from labeled datasets to improve structured clustering and segmentation.

paragraphs: In second-price auctions with a reserve, the choice of reserve price is a central way to influence revenue. This makes reserve selection an important decision for online businesses whose income depends on auction outcomes. The paper treats that decision as a learning problem, making revenue optimization the objective of the learning procedure.

A major challenge is the shape of the corresponding loss function: it is both non-convex and discontinuous. These properties complicate the theoretical analysis and the design of algorithms for selecting a reserve. The authors provide a full theoretical treatment that addresses those properties and introduce algorithms for solving the resulting learning problem.

The paper also reports encouraging experimental evidence for the algorithms' effectiveness. Its contribution combines a formal account of a difficult objective with concrete procedures for optimizing it. The results support learning reserve prices as a practical approach to influencing auction revenue, while the empirical claim remains one of effectiveness in the reported experiments rather than a universal revenue guarantee.
icml-2014-learning-theory-and-algorithms.tldr: The paper develops learning theory and algorithms for revenue-maximizing reserve selection despite a non-convex, discontinuous auction loss.

paragraphs: Hashing-based inference and counting methods use randomized functions to learn about high-dimensional sets that have compact descriptions. Standard constructions offer useful statistical guarantees, but the hash constraints themselves can make inference computationally difficult. This paper targets that obstacle by using sparse parity constraints inspired by low-density parity-check codes.

The proposed constraints belong to a new class called Average Universal hash functions. They do not satisfy the stronger universality property of conventional constructions. The authors nevertheless show that this weaker class preserves the statistical guarantees needed by most of the relevant probabilistic inference methods. The analysis establishes that those methods can retain provable accuracy while using more tractable constraints.

In practice, the change makes a number of algorithms significantly more scalable. The authors use it to obtain tighter bounds on challenging discrete integration and model-counting problems. The contribution shows that a weaker hashing property can be sufficient for the desired inference guarantees, allowing computational improvements without abandoning the accuracy guarantees established for the applicable methods.
icml-2014-low-density-parity-constraints.tldr: Sparse Average Universal hash constraints preserve useful accuracy guarantees while making discrete integration and model counting more scalable.

paragraphs: Infinite hidden Markov models extend ordinary hidden Markov models with an unbounded state space. This makes them flexible descriptions of sequences, but their generative formulation can limit performance when the goal is discriminative prediction. The paper introduces max-margin infinite HMMs to bring a prediction-oriented learning principle into that flexible Bayesian framework.

The authors develop efficient beam sampling algorithms using Gibbs classifier theory and data augmentation. Their inference approach avoids restrictive mean-field assumptions and truncated approximations. For single-variate classification, the model reduces to a new form of Dirichlet process mixture of max-margin machines, connecting the sequential model to a related classification construction.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report better performance than the evaluated competitors for both single-variate classification and sequential prediction. These results support combining flexible latent-state modeling with a discriminative objective. The contribution includes both the new model and an inference method that works without the particular simplifying approximations identified in the abstract.
icml-2014-max-margin-infinite-hidden-mar.tldr: Max-margin infinite HMMs combine Bayesian state-space flexibility with discriminative learning and efficient inference without truncation or mean-field assumptions.

paragraphs: Point-process data describe events through their arrival times, and arrivals across multiple channels can be correlated. The paper models those relationships using hidden external events that appear and disappear over time. This provides a probabilistic account of observed arrivals in terms of underlying activity that is not directly observed.

The hidden activity is represented by a collection of continuous-time binary semi-Markov processes. Each process captures an external event's presence or absence. Working in continuous time avoids the need to divide observations into time bins, an approach the authors argue is less appropriate for multichannel point-process data. They also establish connections to related ideas developed in discrete time.

An efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm performs posterior inference for the model. The authors apply the framework to synthetic data and a real-world biometrics problem. These applications illustrate how correlated arrival data can be analyzed through latent event dynamics while preserving a continuous-time representation. The abstract presents a modeling and inference contribution without claiming a particular comparative performance improvement.
icml-2014-modeling-correlated-arrival-ev.tldr: Latent continuous-time semi-Markov processes explain correlated arrivals through hidden events that switch between presence and absence.

paragraphs: Random MAP perturbations connect optimization with probabilistic sampling: maximizing a randomly perturbed potential can generate unbiased samples from a Gibbs distribution. In high-dimensional models, however, producing the required random variables can be prohibitively expensive. More efficient sequential sampling methods instead rely on expected values of lower-dimensional MAP perturbations.

Those expectations must themselves be estimated from samples. The paper develops concentration inequalities that bound how many samples are needed for these estimates. This addresses a computational ingredient of the sequential strategy: determining how accurately Monte Carlo estimates approximate the expectations on which the sampler depends.

Applying the bounds to MAP perturbations can yield a more efficient approximate Gibbs sampler. The abstract presents this as a possible algorithmic benefit, rather than an unconditional speed guarantee. The concentration result is also more general than this application and may help other problems involving Monte Carlo estimation of expectations. Its broader significance lies in controlling estimation uncertainty in calculations that support probabilistic inference.
icml-2014-on-measure-concentration-of-ra.tldr: New concentration inequalities control estimation of MAP-perturbation expectations and can improve approximate sampling from Gibbs distributions.

paragraphs: Topic models such as LDA discover hidden themes from patterns of word co-occurrence. This paper observes that semantic and syntactic relationships also create strong dependencies between words' topics. It uses those relationships to motivate a model that represents more of the structure connecting words within sentences.

Sentences are represented as dependency trees, and a Global Topic Random Field models nonlinear topical dependencies. The authors define a global factor over all tree edges and prove that the random field's normalization factor is constant. This result supports inference without the independence assumption discussed in the abstract. They then derive an efficient expectation-maximization procedure for estimating model parameters.

Experiments on four datasets find substantially lower perplexity than LDA and linear dependency topic models, together with better topic coherence. These findings support incorporating richer word relationships into topic discovery. The contribution connects a structured representation of sentences with an inference construction that makes those dependencies manageable, and the reported benefits concern both predictive fit and the coherence of the resulting topics.
icml-2014-on-modelling-non-linear-topica.tldr: A Global Topic Random Field uses sentence dependency trees to model nonlinear topical relationships and improves perplexity and topic coherence in experiments.

paragraphs: Passive-Aggressive learning is an online framework for learning large-margin predictors. Its conventional formulation estimates one deterministic model, which can limit the structures it uncovers in complex data. This paper develops a Bayesian version that includes ordinary Passive-Aggressive learning while extending it to richer probabilistic models.

BayesPA naturally accommodates latent variables and nonparametric Bayesian inference. These extensions allow the framework to represent hidden structure and address model complexity within the learning process. The authors apply it to topic modeling, deriving efficient online algorithms for max-margin topic models. They also develop nonparametric methods to determine the number of topics.

Experiments on real datasets show substantial gains in time efficiency while maintaining results comparable to batch counterparts. The findings support online learning as a practical way to fit these structured Bayesian predictors. The main contribution is a unified framework that combines large-margin online updates with latent representations, illustrated by topic models that can also resolve how many topics to use.
icml-2014-online-bayesian-passive-aggres.tldr: Bayesian Passive-Aggressive learning extends online large-margin methods to latent and nonparametric models, improving training efficiency for topic modeling.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to allocate a limited budget to maximize influence in a bipartite model. It places this problem within a broader optimization framework: maximizing a monotone submodular function over integer allocations subject to a knapsack constraint. The framework also covers versions that include a competitor and costs.

For this general problem, the authors provide a (1-1/e)-approximation algorithm. This gives a guaranteed fraction of the optimal objective value rather than a claim of exact optimization. Under the additional condition that influence probabilities are nonincreasing, they obtain a faster algorithm with the same approximation guarantee and runtime essentially linear in the number of nodes.

The reported implementation reaches almost ten million edges. The abstract also gives an experiment-based projection that a billion-edge problem could take approximately 500 seconds; that is a projected capability rather than a stated completed run. The contribution combines a broad mathematical formulation, a provable approximation, and a faster conditional method aimed at making large influence-allocation problems practical.
icml-2014-optimal-budget-allocation-theo.tldr: A general budget-allocation framework yields a (1-1/e) approximation, with an essentially linear-time variant under nonincreasing influence probabilities.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions when obtaining information is restricted or costly. In prediction with limited advice, a learner may consult only M of N experts on each round. The authors provide an algorithm with a regret guarantee that explicitly reflects this restricted access, connecting prediction performance to the amount of advice available.

The second problem allows observations of any number of arms in an adversarial bandit game, but charges a cost for each observation. The algorithm must account for information acquisition as part of its decision problem. The paper gives a worst-case regret bound involving the observation cost, number of arms, and number of rounds, with a leading time dependence of T to the two-thirds power.

Further variants accommodate costs that differ across arms and over time, and achieve lower regret under benign conditions. Lower bounds show that the worst-case guarantees cannot be improved apart from logarithmic factors. Together, the results characterize both achievable performance and fundamental limits when learning must operate with an explicit information budget.
icml-2014-prediction-with-limited-advice.tldr: Algorithms and matching lower bounds characterize online learning when expert advice is limited or observing bandit rewards has a cost.

paragraphs: Bayesian models often incorporate domain knowledge through a prior distribution. This paper offers a more direct route: express knowledge as first-order logic rules and impose those rules on the posterior distribution. The regularized Bayesian framework provides the machinery for combining logical statements with probabilistic learning.

Human-provided rules can differ in reliability, so the method also estimates their uncertainty automatically. Reliable rules are incorporated, while unreliable ones are ignored. This selective treatment matters because the model should benefit from useful knowledge without giving every supplied statement the same influence. Reliability assessment is therefore part of the proposed integration of logic and Bayesian modeling.

The authors apply the approach to latent topic modeling in both unsupervised and supervised learning. They report improved task performance and more structured latent representations from combining the two sources of information. These findings suggest that logical knowledge can influence both prediction-related outcomes and the organization of hidden topics when its reliability is assessed within the framework.
icml-2014-robust-regbayes-selectively-in.tldr: Robust RegBayes incorporates reliable logical rules into Bayesian posteriors while estimating and filtering unreliable human-provided knowledge.

paragraphs: Metropolis-Hastings sampling can become expensive on large datasets because its accept-or-reject decision requires likelihood evaluation across the data. This paper proposes an approximate version of that decision using a random subset. Adaptive subsampling aims to reduce the amount of data processed while retaining explicit probabilistic control over the decision.

The method guarantees that the subsampled decision agrees with the full-data decision with probability above a user-specified tolerance level. This is a probability guarantee, so disagreement remains possible. The authors also establish a distribution-level result: the approximate algorithm samples from a perturbed target distribution whose total variation distance from the intended target is explicitly controlled.

These two guarantees connect a local computational shortcut to its effect on the sampling distribution. The paper examines benefits and limitations through several examples. Its contribution is therefore a controlled approximation to Metropolis-Hastings, giving a way to reason about both reduced likelihood computation and the distributional error introduced by using only part of the data.
icml-2014-towards-scaling-up-markov-chai.tldr: Adaptive subsampling reduces Metropolis-Hastings likelihood work while explicitly controlling decision agreement and deviation from the target distribution.

paragraphs: Tracking requires a controller to make a system follow a target over time. This paper studies linear systems with quadratic losses when the targets may be chosen adversarially. Performance is measured through regret relative to an optimal linear policy, asking how much additional loss the learning controller accumulates over successive rounds.

For adversarial tracking targets, the authors give an efficient algorithm with regret growing as O(log² T). The guarantee holds under standard conditions on the linear system. Its slow growth means the cumulative performance gap to the comparison policy increases only polylogarithmically with the number of rounds, within the stated setting and assumptions.

The paper separately considers adversarially chosen transition dynamics, where the system's evolution itself can vary adversarially. It provides an exponentially weighted averaging algorithm with O(√T) regret bounds for that problem. These results distinguish uncertainty in the target from adversarial variation in the dynamics, and provide different algorithms and guarantees for the two control settings.
icml-2014-tracking-adversarial-targets-8.tldr: The paper gives low-regret algorithms for linear control with adversarial targets and, separately, adversarial transition dynamics.

paragraphs: Some learning problems attach entire histograms or probability distributions to observations, rather than single labels. Product ratings and traffic measurements are examples mentioned in this paper. The authors develop graph-based semi-supervised learning for such data, using known histograms at labeled nodes to support learning elsewhere on the graph.

The method is derived from optimal transportation theory. Its behavior can be characterized through the moments and shapes of the labeled histograms, connecting the propagation process to meaningful properties of the distributions being learned. This gives a way to describe how the supplied distributional information affects the method, beyond treating each histogram as an undifferentiated collection of numbers.

The approach also accommodates histograms on nonstandard domains such as circles. That extension reveals a strategy for semi-supervised learning with values on manifolds. The authors further extend the technique to smoothing distributions attached to graph nodes. The contribution is thus a distribution-aware graph learning method with both structural characterizations and related extensions.
icml-2014-wasserstein-propagation-for-se.tldr: Wasserstein propagation uses optimal transportation to learn and smooth graph-associated histograms, including distributions on circular domains.
